Lock APIlock() and unlock(): one key on the table

    

      
mutex_t lk = MUTEX_INIT();

      
void T_sum(int tid) {

      
  for (int i = 0; i < N / 10; i++) {

      
    mutex_lock(&lk);        // take the key

      
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)

      
      sum++;                // ten loads, adds, stores

      
    mutex_unlock(&lk);      // put it back

      
  }

      
}

Peterson1965 to 1981: locks from loads and stores

    
Edsger W. Dijkstrapublished Dekker's algorithm, 1965

    
Dekker's rule · 1965A process P can enter the critical section if the other does not want to enter, otherwise it may enter only if it is its turn.

    
Peterson's rule · 1981A process P can enter the critical section if the other does not want to enter, or it has indicated its desire to enter and has given the other process the turn.

    
G. L. Peterson, "Myths about the mutual exclusion problem"Information Processing Letters, 1981 · only loads and stores, two threads

    
Each rule fits in one sentence, and neither one is obviously right

    
Photo: Hamilton Richards, CC BY-SA 3.0 · rule sentences as quoted in the source lecture

  

  

    

    
PetersonTwo flags and a note on the door

    
    
To enter: 1 raise your flag · 2 put the other's name on the door · 3 wait while the other's flag is up and the door names the other

    
To leave: lower your flag (leave the note)

    

    
Whoever posts the note last waits: it looks polite, but the first to post goes first

    
Peterson's protocol told as a single-occupancy restroom, after the source lecture · A and B stand for the two threads

  

  

    

    
PetersonPeterson in code, one step per click

    

      
void T_A() {

      
  while (1) {

      
    a = 1;

      
    turn = B;

      
    while (1) {

      
      if (!b) break;

      
      if (turn != B) break;

      
    }

      
    critical_section();

      
    a = 0;

      
  }

      
}

    

    

      
void T_B() {

      
  while (1) {

      
    b = 1;

      
    turn = A;

      
    while (1) {

      
      if (!a) break;

      
      if (turn != A) break;

      
    }

      
    critical_section();

      
    b = 0;

      
  }

      
}

PetersonWhy A and B cannot both be inside

    

    

    
The argument needs every write to happen in program orderkeep this in mind: real CPUs break it

    
Whoever writes turn last must wait, so both can never be inside

    
Proof sketch by contradiction for peterson.c (T_A, T_B), assuming loads and stores happen at once and in program order

  

  

    

    
CheckerProof by brute force: visit every state

    

      
queue, vertices = [s0], {s0.name: s0}

      
while queue:

      
    u, queue = queue[0], queue[1:]

      
    for chosen, _ in enumerate(threads):

      
        v = State(Class, u.trace + [chosen])  # one step

      
        if v.name not in vertices:

      
            queue.append(v)

      
            vertices[v.name] = v

RealityOn x86, Peterson breaks in 2 seconds

    
./peterson  (BARRIER empty), 3 runs
run 1: exit -6 after 2.34 s: Assertion failed: (atomic_fetch_add(&inside, +1) == 0)
run 2: exit -6 after 1.26 s: Assertion failed: (atomic_fetch_add(&inside, -1) == 1)
run 3: exit -6 after 1.76 s: Assertion failed: (atomic_fetch_add(&inside, -1) == 1)

    

    
The proof assumed program order; x86 lets a load pass a store

    
peterson.c from the source lecture's demos, run on this laptop (Intel i5-7360U), 20 s limit per run · store buffer after x86-TSO (Sewell et al., Communications of the ACM, 2010)

  

  

    

    
RealityFences fix it, for two threads

    
BARRIER EMPTY · objdump of T_A

    

      
movl  $1, _a           # a = 1

      
movl  $2, (%rax)       # turn = B

      
cmpl  $0, _b           # if (!b)

      
je    enter

      
movl  (%rax), %edx     # load turn

      
cmpl  $2, %edx

      
je    retry

    

    
BARRIER = __sync_synchronize()

    

      
movl  $1, _a           # a = 1

      
mfence

      
movl  $2, (%rax)       # turn = B

      
mfence

      
cmpl  $0, _b           # if (!b)

      
je    enter

      
mfence

      
movl  (%rax), %edx     # load turn

      
cmpl  $2, %edx

      
je    retry

    

    
The same fence:x86: mfenceARM: dmb ishRISC-V: fence rw, rw

    
And Peterson serves only two threadseach one must know the other's name; real programs create threads at will

    
Correct Peterson needs a fence after every step, and still serves only two threads

    
Disassembly (llvm objdump) of T_A in peterson.c compiled with clang -O2 on this laptop, both versions; labels and comments ours; fence names per the source lecture

  

  

    

    
AtomicChange the rules: one indivisible step

    
Intel 80486, 1989the lock prefix drives the LOCK# pin

    
    
lock addq $1, sum

    
Every ISA has them:x86: lock add, lock xchg, lock cmpxchgARM: ldxr / stxr, ldaddRISC-V: lr / sc, amoadd, amoswap

    
Today the core locks one cache line, not the whole bus

    
Hardware gives one indivisible read-modify-write, and that is all a lock needs

    
Photo: yellowcloud, CC BY 2.0 · blocks and the LOCK# signal after "80486DX2 arch.svg" by Appaloosa and Lucid, CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons), redrawn · instruction names per the source lecture

  

  

    

    
Atomiclock addq: 1 + 1 = 2 again

    

      
void *Tsum(void *arg) {

      
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) {

      
        asm volatile("lock addq $1, %0": "+m"(x));

      
        // asm volatile("addq $1, %0": "+m"(x));

      
    }

      
    return NULL;

      
}
